Wednesday-Monday: The Eastern Pacific is energized and several 
storm systems will impact the PacNW into next week. There are 
two distinct storm systems that we will be focusing on for this 
period. The first will impact the region Wednesday night into 
Thursday with the second Saturday into Monday. Now that the 
atmosphere has modified into a cool, Pacific maritime air mass, 
a bulk of the precipitation will fall in the lowlands will be 
rain. Snow will impact some mountain passes at times and 
potentially the northern mountains and we will dive further into
this below. If you are looking for generally dry conditions, 
first will be today (WED) once a band of very light rain exits 
early this morning. Next will be Friday, though rain chances 
will be on the increase from the south as the day progresses. 

Wednesday night-Thursday: A strong Pacific jet nosing across the 
dateline is driving a robust low pressure toward the WA Coast 
which will steer a plume of subtropical moisture into the 
region. Precipitation will increase over the Cascades Wednesday 
evening and expand eastward toward the Idaho Panhandle Wednesday
night into Thursday morning ahead of a strengthening warm 
front. The trailing cold front will sweep through during the day
on Thursday bringing an end to the precipitation in the lee of 
the Cascades and across the Basin but orographic showers will 
pick back up as gusty southwest winds develop. Moderate QPF 
amounts 0.25-0.50 inches are forecast for the northern tier of 
Idaho and Washington with amounts between a 0.10-0.20 inches 
into the lower Basin. Heavier amounts, closer to an inch or 
more, are forecast for the Cascade Crest. 

Snow impacts: Snow levels will be rising slowly Wednesday 
afternoon into the evening climbing between 5000-6000 feet. The
two areas of concern for snow to impact travel are 1) 
Washington Pass and 2) Sherman Pass. My confidence is moderate 
to high that Washington Pass will pick up copious amounts of 
snow having moderate to major impacts over the pass. My 
confidence for Sherman Pass is moderate to low. Guidance is 
indicating a 80% chance for p-type to remain snow at the pass 
level with over a three tenths of an inch of QPF but only 
indicating an inch or two of snow. This suggest the ratios could
be very wet but in past events, these heavy wet snow events can
lead to moderate impacts or greater if intensities are high 
enough. Winter storm warnings have been issued for Washington 
Pass with a foot of snow expected. We will continue to analyze 
conditions at Sherman and determine if winter weather advisories
are necessary given the increase holiday travel impacts for 
Thursday morning. The upper Methow Valley will be another area 
that could experience impacts from wet snow. Thermal profiles 
will be real close to the 0C isotherm and if the precip 
intensity is high enough, this could fall as wet, heavy snow vs 
rain with snow ranges in the models from 0 to 8 inches. 

Wind: A light southeast to east wind on Wednesday will become 
breezy Wednesday night with gusts increasing 20-30 mph from the
Palouse to the Okanogan Valley. As the cold front comes through
around midday Thursday, winds shift to the southwest and wind 
speeds will increase across the wind prone Basin and into the 
Spokane Area with speeds of 15 to 20 mph coupled with gusts 
25-30 mph. Higher peaks across the Cascades and into the Idaho 
Panhandle will experience gusts closer to 35-40 mph. 

Friday-Monday:  System one will be in the rear view mirror 
Friday morning and we will start to see impacts from the next 
system. The next deep low crossing into the E Pac will bring 
height rises toward the Coast. The axis of subtropical moisture 
that arrived with the Thursday system will still be in play and 
continue to be primed with additional subtropical moisture from 
offshore. This axis of moisture will lay over the top of the 
building ridge and stretch across the Inland NW as a pseudo 
stationary warm front. This will result in increasing clouds and
areas of widespread precipitation starting from south and 
expand northward from Friday afternoon and into Saturday. Given 
some cooling in the wake of Thursday's cold front, this will 
lead to a trickier forecast for snow on the Cascade passes with 
Stevens likely to start off as snow. Some of the upper Cascade 
river valleys and northern mountain and mountain valleys may 
also be cold enough to support wet snow but there is a lower 
chance for this moisture to expand as far north as Highway 20 on
Friday.

Monday. There are a lot of different scenarios with the
